scope.start: 2a: the opening Mishnah of the tractate, *ha-isha nikneit bi-shalosh derachim*

sections.title: The Mishnah: How a Woman Is Acquired and Released
sections.gist: The opening mishnah lists three ways a woman is betrothed and two ways she goes free, sets the minimum *kesef*, and applies the same frame to the *yevamah*.

chart.caption: The Mishnah's two cases: how each is acquired and how she acquires herself
rows: A bill of divorce, or the husband's death

children.title: Three Ways In, Two Ways Out: Kesef, Shtar, Bi'ah
children.gist: A woman is betrothed through money, a document or *bi'ah* (intercourse), and she "acquires herself" in two ways, which means she becomes free to marry another man.

bullets.text: Mishnah: *ha-isha nikneit bi-shalosh derachim, ve-konah et atzmah bi-shtei derachim*. She is acquired through *kesef*, *shtar* and *bi'ah*.
Rashi: *konah et atzmah* means she comes under her own control, free to marry another man. That is the core bond *kiddushin* creates, and its dissolution is what "acquiring herself" means.
*Kesef*: giving an object of value with the words *harei at mekudeshet li*, before witnesses. The witnesses don't merely prove the act; they make it legally binding, as with *gittin*.
The ring appears in neither the Bavli nor the Yerushalmi. It is first recorded in the Geonic-era *Sefer ha-Chilukim*, which reports that Eretz Yisrael used a ring and the Jews of Bavel did not.
*Shtar*: a document reading *harei at mekudeshet li*, handed to her before witnesses. It is fully valid, yet there is no evidence it was used in practice; the Gemara's stories are all about *kesef*.

The *ketubah* is not the *shtar*, and *yichud* is not the *bi'ah*: both belong to *nisu'in*. Some Genizah *ketubot* (studied by Mordechai Friedman) do include *harei at mekudeshet li*, suggesting a conceptual blurring in some communities.
*Bi'ah*: a single act of intercourse done with the intent to create *kiddushin*, not any act of intimacy.
The first *perek* is about *kinyanim* broadly: the woman, the *yevamah*, the *eved ivri*, the *eved kena'ani*, land and movables, each named with its modes of acquisition.

children.title: Kiddushin versus Nisu'in
children.gist: *Kiddushin* creates the legal status of a married woman, while living together, the household and the mutual obligations begin only with *nisu'in*.

bullets.text: After *kiddushin*, another man's *kiddushin* has no effect, relations with another man are adultery, and she needs a *get* to leave. But the couple does not yet share a home or a life.
*Nisu'in* (the *chuppah*), treated in Ketubot, brings *she'er, kesut ve-onah* and, in the other direction, her earnings to her husband.
The stages could be years apart. In arranged matches the binding mechanism was originally *kiddushin* itself (later, *tna'im* with penalties), and *nisu'in* followed once the girl had grown up.
This explains Rashi's precision. He mentions only her freedom to marry another, not vows or earnings, because those flow from *nisu'in*, not from *kiddushin*.
The *bi'ah* of *kiddushin* is a one-time legal act, entirely different in kind from the ongoing relationship of *nisu'in*.

children.title: Kesef: A Dinar or a Perutah
children.gist: Beit Shammai require a *dinar*'s worth and Beit Hillel a *perutah*'s worth, and the mishnah fixes the *perutah* at one-eighth of an Italian *issar*.

bullets.text: Beit Shammai: a *dinar* or anything worth a *dinar*. Beit Hillel: a *perutah*, a small copper coin, or anything worth a *perutah*.
How much is a *perutah*, by the fixed value of silver? One-eighth of the Italian *issar*.
"Or its equivalent" means the object need not be a coin at all. Since Beit Hillel's *perutah* is itself copper, *kesef* here cannot literally mean silver; it simply means value.

The mishnah is layered. The core, *nikneit be-kesef, be-shtar u-ve-vi'ah*, is terse. The Beit Shammai–Beit Hillel dispute is a gloss asking what *kesef* means, and the *perutah*'s definition is a gloss on the gloss.

Without the gloss, *kesef* would naturally mean a real price, like the Torah's fifty-silver *mohar*. That sum migrated to the *ketubah* (200 *zuz*), payable at death or divorce, which left the upfront payment symbolic and raised the question of how little suffices.
Contrast land, acquired through *kesef, shtar u-chazakah*. There *kesef* means the market price; nobody buys a house for a *perutah*.

Two models of marriage run through the *perek*. In the *kinyan* model the man acquires something in her, such as sexual rights. In the *kiddushin* model marriage is a personal status of exclusivity that arises from a relationship.
Signs of the *kinyan* model: the husband's duty of *onah* is derived from a verse, while the wife's duty is simply assumed; and damages for a miscarriage are paid to the husband.
Every mishnah in the tractate uses the language of *kiddushin* except this first one. Once the payment became a symbol, the institution was no longer called *kinyan* but *kiddushin*.

children.title: Her Release, and the Yevamah
children.gist: A wife goes free through a *get* or her husband's death, and a *yevamah* is acquired only through *bi'ah* and freed by *chalitzah* or the *yavam*'s death.

bullets.text: A woman acquires herself through a bill of divorce or through the death of her husband.
A *yevamah* is acquired by the *yavam* only through *bi'ah*.
She acquires herself, released from the levirate bond, through *chalitzah* or through the death of the *yavam*.

sections.title: Nikneit, Not Mekadesh: Why This Mishnah Speaks of Acquisition
sections.gist: This mishnah says "a woman is acquired" while chapter two says "a man betroths"; the Gemara explains the verb, the later change of language and the choice of the woman as subject.

children.title: Because of Kesef: Kicha–Kicha from Efron's Field
children.gist: The mishnah uses acquisition language because it teaches betrothal with money, which is learned by *gezerah shavah* from Avraham's purchase of Efron's field.

bullets.text: Question: why does this mishnah say *ha-isha nikneit*, while the next chapter (42a) says *ha-ish mekadesh*?
Answer: the *tanna* wants to teach betrothal with money, the standard means of acquisition, so he uses the language of acquisition.

The source for money is a *gezerah shavah*, *kicha–kicha*: "*Ki yikach ish isha*" (Devarim 24:1) and "*Natati kesef ha-sadeh, kach mimeni*" (Bereishit 23:13). Just as Efron's field was acquired with money, so too a woman.
And the taking of the field is called acquisition: "*ha-sadeh asher kanah Avraham*" (Bereishit 25:10).
Alternatively, buying fields with money is called acquisition in "*sadot ba-kesef yiknu*" (Yirmeyahu 32:44). So the *tanna*, teaching money, said "is acquired."
Tosafot: the Yirmeyahu verse also shows that the money itself performs the acquisition, and is not merely a price paid alongside some other act, such as *chazakah*.

children.title: Tosafot's Two Questions on the Gezerah Shavah
children.gist: Tosafot ask why the Efron derivation is needed at all, and point out that its "taking" refers to the money rather than the field.

bullets.text: First question: if we already know money is the means, why bring the whole Efron parallel to show that *kiddushin* is a *kinyan*?
Answer: money by itself need not mean *kinyan*. It could work through some other mechanism. The *gezerah shavah* makes the *kesef* of *kiddushin* a *kinyan* in the same sense as buying a field.
Second question: in Bereishit 23:13 what is "taken" is the money, whereas in Devarim 24:1 it is the woman herself. The parallel is imperfect.
The Torah's language of "taking" a woman fits the *mohar* framework, in which her father gives her and she is the object of the transaction rather than its subject.

children.title: Kicha in the Torah Means Nisu'in; Betrothal Is Eirus
children.gist: In the Torah's own usage "taking" a woman means full marriage, while betrothal is *eirus*, so Chazal learn *kiddushin* from verses whose plain sense is *nisu'in*.

bullets.text: Tosafot: "*ve-ish asher yikach et achoto*" refers to relations, not betrothal. In "*ki yikach ish isha u-va eileha*" the taking is bringing her into his household, and the relations simply follow.
The Torah's word for betrothal is *eiras*: "*mi ha-ish asher eiras isha ve-lo lekachah*." *Eirus* comes first, and taking comes afterward.
The paradox: Chazal derive *kiddushin* mainly from the *kicha* verses, which in their plain sense describe *nisu'in*.
The Torah's *kinyan* model grows out of the *mohar* paid to the father at *eirus*, not out of the word *kicha* itself.

children.title: Torah Language First, Rabbinic Language After
children.gist: Chapter two does not say "a man acquires" because the first mishnah speaks the Torah's language and the later one the Sages', who call betrothal *kiddushin*.

bullets.text: Question: then let the next chapter also say "a man acquires."
Answer: *me-ikara tani lishna de-Oraita, u-le-vasof tani lishna de-Rabbanan*. It opens with the Torah's language, in which betrothal is "taking," and later uses the Sages' language.
The change of words is not arbitrary. It tracks a real conceptual shift from *kinyan* to *kiddushin*.

children.title: Why "Kiddushin": Forbidden to All Like Hekdesh
children.gist: The Sages' term means that the husband makes her forbidden to everyone, like consecrated property, and Tosafot add that the word *li* grounds this in her bond to him.

bullets.text: Betrothal is called *kiddushin* *de-asar lah a-kulei alma ke-hekdesh*: he renders her forbidden to everyone like consecrated property.
The analogy is imperfect. *Hekdesh* is forbidden to its owner too, and one can consecrate only what one already owns. Neither is true of a wife.
Tosafot on *harei at mekudeshet li*: just as "sanctified to Heaven" means belonging to Heaven and so forbidden to all else, *li* means she is forbidden to everyone because she is bound to him.
The shift is from possession to a status that arises from a relationship. The man still initiates. *Hekdesh* itself can be read as dedication rather than a transfer of ownership to God.

children.title: Why the Woman Is the Subject
children.gist: The mishnah says "the woman is acquired" rather than "the man acquires" because it goes on to "she acquires herself", or, alternatively, to teach that betrothal requires her consent.

bullets.text: Question: let this mishnah also say "a man acquires."
Answer: the latter clause says "and she acquires herself," about her, so the first clause also speaks about her.
Then say "the man acquires and releases (*koneh u-makneh*)." No: when the husband dies, it is not he who releases her; her freedom comes from Heaven.
Alternatively, "the man acquires" would suggest he can acquire her even against her will. "The woman is acquired" teaches: with her consent, yes; without her consent, no.
The whole *perek* is organized around the thing acquired (woman, *yevamah*, slaves, land), so naming the object also fits its pattern.
In the Torah a father married off his daughter without asking her; Rivkah being consulted is the exception. Chazal limited the father's power to a minor.
At its very first use, the vocabulary of acquisition is turned into an affirmation of her agency: she is a subject whose consent is required, not only an object.

sections.title: Bi-Shalosh Derachim: Why This Wording
sections.gist: The Gemara asks two questions about the mishnah's phrase: why the feminine *shalosh*, and why "ways" at all rather than "matters".

children.title: Shalosh, Not Shelosha: The Gender of Derech
children.gist: *Derech* is feminine, yet verses and mishnayot also treat it as masculine, and the Gemara resolves both conflicts by context.

chart.caption: When *derech* is feminine and when masculine
rows: Refers to the Torah, which is feminine (*temimah*)
Refers to war, the way of a man
Examining a *zav* applies to a man

children.title: Feminine Here, Masculine There: The Contradictions
children.gist: Shemot 18:20 shows *derech* is feminine, but Devarim 28:7 and the *zav* mishnah use the masculine, so both the verses and the mishnayot seem to clash.

bullets.text: Why *shalosh* and not *shelosha*? Because the mishnah wants the word *derech*, which is feminine: "*ve-hoda'ta lahem et ha-derech yelchu vah*" (Shemot 18:20).

But the mishnah in Nazir (65b) says *bi-shiv'ah derachim bodkin et ha-zav*, in the masculine. Answer: *derech* is also masculine: "*be-derech echad yetz'u eilecha u-ve-shiv'ah derachim yanusu lefanecha*" (Devarim 28:7).
If so, the verses contradict each other, and the mishnayot contradict each other.

children.title: Context Decides: Torah and War, Woman and Zav
children.gist: A *derech* of Torah is feminine and a *derech* of war masculine; likewise the mishnah about a woman uses the feminine and the one about examining a *zav* the masculine.

bullets.text: Shemot 18:20 speaks of the way of Torah, and Torah is feminine: "*Torat Hashem temimah*" (Tehillim 19:8).
Devarim 28:7 speaks of war, and it is the way of a man to wage war, not of a woman, so the masculine fits.
Our mishnah speaks of a woman, so it uses the feminine.

The *zav* mishnah uses the masculine because a man is examined to see whether his emission had another cause. A woman is not examined: she is impure even from a discharge beyond her control, so its cause does not matter.

illustration.caption: The Gemara's resolution: the way of Torah (Shemot 18:20) is feminine, the ways of war (Devarim 28:7) masculine; so too our mishnah about a woman uses *shalosh*, while the mishnah about examining a *zav* uses *shiv'ah*.

children.title: Derachim, Not Devarim: Why "Ways" at All
children.gist: If the word *derech* forces the feminine, why not say *devarim* ("matters")? The Gemara tests explanations for "ways" in this mishnah and in others.

children.title: *Bi'ah* Is Called a Way
children.gist: The mishnah says "ways" because Mishlei calls *bi'ah* a *derech*, and money and document follow suit because they too serve the marital bond.

bullets.text: Question: then let it say *shelosha devarim*, three matters, in the masculine. Answer: it wanted to include *bi'ah*, which is called a way: "the way of a man with a young woman; so is the way of an adulterous woman" (Mishlei 30:19–20).
And money and document? Since *bi'ah* had to be called a way, the mishnah used "way" for the other two as well.
Would the mishnah phrase two cases for the sake of one? Money and document too are for the sake of *bi'ah*: the marital relationship is the purpose of betrothal.

children.title: R. Shimon: A Man Seeks What He Lost
children.gist: Alternatively, the mishnah follows R. Shimon, who explains that the Torah says "when a man takes" because it is the *derech* of a man to pursue a woman.

bullets.text: Alternatively, the mishnah follows R. Shimon's *baraita*. Why does the Torah say "*ki yikach ish isha*" (Devarim 22:13) and not "when a woman is taken by a man"? Because it is the way of a man to pursue a woman, and not the way of a woman to pursue a man.
A parable: when someone loses an item, who searches for whom? The owner searches for his lost item. Woman was created from man's side, so the man seeks what he lost.

illustration.caption: R. Shimon's *baraita* (2b): the Torah says "when a man takes a woman" because it is a man's way to pursue a woman, just as the owner of a lost item searches for it.

children.title: The Zav: Eating and Drinking as "Ways"
children.gist: The *zav* mishnah says "ways" to teach that excessive eating or drinking is a way that leads to *zivah*.

bullets.text: Why does the mishnah say "one examines a *zav* in seven ways" and not "matters"? To teach that excessive eating is a way that leads to *zivah*, and so is excessive drinking.

returns_to.note: Returns to the *zav* mishnah (Nazir 65b), now asking about the word "ways" rather than its gender

children.title: The Etrog: Like a Tree in Three Ways, Like a Vegetable in One
children.gist: Bikkurim 2:6 says "ways" because of its last clause, and the Gemara asks why that clause too does not say "matter"; the answer comes on 3a.

bullets.text: Mishnah (Bikkurim 2:6): the *etrog* is like a tree in three ways. Why not "matters"? Because the latter clause says it is like a vegetable in one way, the first clause says "ways" too.
Then let the latter clause say "one matter"!

children.continues: Continues on 3a: the *etrog*, like a vegetable, is watered by all water and tithed by its harvest time. Then the *koy* and *gittin* mishnayot lead the Gemara to a new rule: "ways" where there is a distinction, "matters" where there is none.

judgment_calls: Kiddushin versus Nisu'in (s3) is entirely shiur framing and could have been folded into the three-ways section; kept as its own child of the Mishnah because it is a distinct conceptual point, and Rashi's precision depends on it.

The kinyan-versus-kiddushin models were placed in the kesef section, where the shiur ties them to the shift from *mohar* to a symbolic payment; they could instead stand as a separate framing section before the Gemara's opening question.

Tosafot's questions (s8) and the kicha-versus-eirus discussion (s9) come later in the lecture, but they comment on the *gezerah shavah*, so they are nested under it (s7) as shiur children rather than placed as separate sections in lecture order.
The consent inference is discussed in the shiur both under the meaning of *kiddushin* and later; it is outlined once, at 2b.5 where the text has it, as the alternative answer in s12.

The "ways versus matters" discussion (s17) could be its own top-level section; grouped with the gender question under one parent (s13) because both interrogate the phrase *bi-shalosh derachim*, and the second question grows out of the first answer.

The Mishnah's release and *yevamah* clauses (s5) were kept as a child of the Mishnah section rather than merged into the three-ways section, so the chart comparing woman and *yevamah* sits on the parent.
coverage_notes: The shiur's overview of the tractate (comparison with Gittin, the content of perakim 2–4, and why Kiddushin follows Ketubot) is outside this daf's text and was left out, except for a brief note on the first perek's structure.
The Mishnah's clauses on release (a *get* or death) and on the *yevamah* are not discussed in the shiur; outlined from the text only (s5).

2b.10–2b.15 (intercourse called *derech*, R. Shimon's baraita, the *zav* and eating and drinking, the *etrog* mishnah) are not discussed in the shiur; outlined from the text only. This is the first daf of the tractate, so there is no previous essay tail.

The essay says the Italian *issar* was a copper coin and builds an argument on it; the text calls the *issar* a small silver coin (the *perutah* is the copper coin). Followed the text and kept only the point that the *perutah* itself is copper.
The essay presents "*sadot ba-kesef yiknu*" (Yirmeyahu 32:44) as a further confirming verse; the text offers it as an alternative proof ("alternatively"). Followed the text.

The essay presents the "structural" focus on the object acquired as the Gemara's answer to why the woman is the subject; the Gemara's answer is that the latter clause says "she acquires herself." Followed the text and kept the structural point as shiur.

The essay discusses the consent inference before the *koneh u-makneh* exchange and says the Gemara is aware of the father's biblical rights; the text's order is *koneh u-makneh* first, then consent as an alternative answer, and the father's rights are not in the text. Followed the text's order and marked the father's rights as shiur.
The essay lists sleep among the causes examined for a *zav*; the text mentions only excessive eating and drinking. Omitted sleep.
